newsitem.title: USA: Dollar continues rally but loses steam in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dollar continues rally but loses steam in U.S.

text.p: The dollar rose broadly again Monday, continuing to benefit from the contrast of sturdy U.S. economic growth against languishing overseas economies.

Extending its 1997 rally, the dollar set a series of fresh multiyear highs after another dramatic drop in Japan's stock market further eroded confidence in Japanese yen investments, while remarks from German central bankers highlighted Germany's economic woes.

But, after reaching 118.29 yen and 1.6315 German marks in European trade, the dollar's best levels since March 1993 and June 1994, respectively, the rally fizzled in the United States where trading desks were thinly staffed in observance of the Martin Luther King Jr holiday.
"There was little bit of action, mostly centred in Europe," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland. "The New York end of things is very quiet."
Trade activity in New York nearly evaporated shortly after noontime. The dollar ended the session at 118.13 yen, up from 117.37 yen Friday and at 1.6285 marks, from 1.6182 marks.
The dollar also scored a 31-month high just over 1.42 swiss francs on Monday, before settling at 1.4180 Swiss francs, up from 1.3993.
Traders are increasingly viewing dollar investments as a can't-lose bet, while evidence that the U.S. economy entered 1997 in excellent fitness continues to mount.
"They do have an appetite to buy dollars on dips," said Susan Stearns, a director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal in New York.
"It appears that those who are buying dollars are also wearing diamonds," she added jokingly.

The latest bits of good news for the United States came Friday when government data on December industrial activity and the November international trade deficit prompted many Wall Street economists to revise their fourth-quarter economic growth forecasts upwards.

At the same time, the ferocious decline in Japan's Nikkei 225 stock average, which dropped another 609.70 points Monday, has prompted selling of Japanese stocks by foreign investors, who continue to convert the yen proceeds into other units like the dollar.

Meanwhile, in an article in the International Herald Tribune on Monday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer drew attention to Germany's economic troubles by warning that Germany's faltering economic recovery had not reached critical mass.
In a speech Monday, another Bundesbank policy-maker, Hans-Juergen Krupp, also chimed in, saying German financial policy is "hindering still-continuing economic recovery."

The remarks bolstered the dollar by fuelling speculation the German central bank may deliver a mark-damaging reduction in a key interest rate, known as the repo, to stimulate the economy. The Bundesbank holds its biweekly policy-setting meeting Thursday.
"Some more weak economic data expected from Germany, which will support potentially another repo cut -- I think that is the idea," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3370 from C$1.3405 on Friday, and the pound fell to $1.6625 from $1.6672.
